messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Authority Presence: Police, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Arjun's World

Arjun Patel sits at his design workstation in the downtown Minneapolis office where he has worked for eight years, his fingers poised over the keyboard but his attention elsewhere. The morning light filters through the windows facing the street, and when a siren passes—a sound that has become increasingly frequent in his awareness—his shoulders tense and his breath catches. He tells himself it is nothing, that he is being irrational, yet his body does not believe him. He has learned not to fight the sensation. Instead, he waits for it to pass, a familiar knot in his chest that loosens only when the sound fades completely. His colleagues have stopped asking why he sometimes closes his office door or why he is reluctant to attend the weekly team lunches in the downtown core.

Eighteen months ago, Arjun's world fractured in a moment he still cannot fully articulate. He had been driving home from a client meeting on a humid July evening when he was pulled over by police for a broken taillight. The interaction itself began ordinarily—the officer's approach, the request for documents—but what followed remains fragmented in his mind, a sequence of events he knows happened but cannot piece together into a coherent narrative. When he tries to explain it to his wife Priya, his words scatter. He knows the officer's hand moved toward something, knows he felt afraid, knows there was shouting, but when he attempts to reconstruct the moments, the thread breaks. The harder he grasps for clarity, the more elusive it becomes. What he carries most vividly is not the sequence but the overwhelming sensation of betrayal—that a person whose role was to protect had instead become a source of terror, and that this person had been someone he had been taught to trust.

Since that night, Arjun has become hyperaware of uniforms. When he sees a police officer at a coffee shop or walking past his office building, his mind immediately catalogs their position, their direction, whether they have noticed him. He finds himself rehearsing conversations in his head before any interaction with authority—the woman at the DMV, the building manager, even his accountant. He scripts what he will say, anticipating accusations or misunderstandings, preparing justifications. The mental rehearsal has become so habitual that he often does not realize he is doing it until Priya asks why he is so quiet, and he realizes he has been silently running through dialogue for the past twenty minutes.

The smell of burnt rubber or burnt plastic now triggers an immediate sense of danger. Last month, when a colleague microwaved something too long in the office kitchen and a burnt smell drifted through the hallway, Arjun felt his body flood with panic. He had to step outside, telling his manager he needed air. He did not explain why a smell had undone him so completely.

What has changed most noticeably in the past year is Arjun's relationship to the future. He and Priya had been discussing taking a sabbatical, perhaps traveling to India to visit family, but he cannot bring himself to make plans. When she suggests booking flights or looking at dates, something in him resists. He has come to believe that the world is fundamentally unsafe, that planning assumes a future he is no longer certain he will have, or that he deserves to have. The guilt that accompanies memories of that night is intense and irrational—he knows he did nothing wrong, yet when the event surfaces in his mind, he is flooded with a sense of culpability, as though he had somehow caused or invited what happened. This guilt makes planning feel like a betrayal of some unspoken penance he owes.

Priya finally insisted he seek help after finding him, late one night, sitting alone in the dark in their bedroom, unable to articulate why he was there or what he needed. He had called in sick to work three times that week, and his manager had begun to ask questions. Arjun now sits in his first therapy session, exhausted by the effort of holding himself together, hoping that someone might help him understand how a single moment has come to define his entire world, and whether he might ever feel safe again.
